commonNameFr.name: Pied-bêche des plaines
commonNameFr.source: NatureServe Explorer (French common names listed: 'Crapaud des plaines', 'Pied-bêche des plaines')

taxonomyNote: Animal Diversity Web places it in Pelobatidae, whereas NatureServe (citing Garcia-Paris et al. 2003) uses Scaphiopodidae for North American spadefoots.
fieldMarks: Vertical (catlike) pupil in bright light and a single hard, wedge-shaped black 'spade' on each hind foot.
Hard raised boss (bony lump) between the eyes, set slightly forward of a line across the middle of both eyes.

Brown or gray, sometimes greenish, with dark splotches and small warts; often an hourglass-like marking formed by four light lines, which can be faint or absent in small animals; some have red or orange spots.
Snout-vent length to about 6 cm (2.5 in); spadefoots are not true toads (Bufonidae).
Breeding males have dark pads on the inner 2-3 fingers; call is a brief, loud, harsh snore audible up to about 3 km.
behavior: Nocturnal: stays in a burrow by day (to about 1 m deep) and emerges on humid nights to forage; burrows deeper in drought, summer heat and winter.
Explosive breeder: 2.5-10.4 cm of rain brings adults to temporary pools, mainly May-August, with choruses lasting about 2 days.
Adults eat small invertebrates; tadpoles may develop a carnivorous morph that eats other tadpoles and fairy shrimp.
Migrates up to several hundred metres between breeding pools and non-breeding ground.
habitat: Shrublands, grasslands and semi-desert with loose soil for burrowing, plus nearby ephemeral pools such as cattle ponds, vernal pools, playas and flooded fields for breeding.
range: South-central Canada (southern Alberta and Saskatchewan, north to near Outlook, SK) south to north-central Mexico, west to western Montana, eastern Colorado and eastern Arizona and east to western Iowa, eastern Missouri and central Arkansas, with disjunct populations in southern Texas and Arkansas.

lookalikes.name: Mexican spadefoot (Spea multiplicata)
lookalikes.howToTell: Lacks the hard boss between the eyes, has red-tipped tubercles, and reportedly smells of peanuts when handled; its call is a longer, stuttering snore.

lookalikes.name: Great Basin spadefoot (Spea intermontana)
lookalikes.howToTell: Separated mainly by range: Great Basin spadefoot lies between the Cascade-Sierra axis and the Rockies, plains spadefoot on the Great Plains.
